nameStory: This spider earned its arrow-shaped name from its distinctive triangular abdomen that looks remarkably like an arrowhead pointing forward. The scientific name sagittata comes from the Latin word for 'arrowed,' making this one of those perfect cases where both the common and scientific names tell the same visual story.
description: The Arrow-shaped Orbweaver is one of New England's most distinctive spiders, instantly recognizable by its bright yellow, triangular abdomen that resembles an arrowhead. This eye-catching spider has six spiky projections (called tubercles) along its abdomen's edges, with the rear pair being especially prominent and forming the arrow's back corners. Females grow to about 9mm long (not counting legs), while males are much smaller at 5mm and lack the dramatic spines. You'll almost always spot the females, as males are rarely seen.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The abdomen is unmistakably triangular and arrow-shaped, wider at the back and tapering to a point at the front, creating a geometric silhouette unlike any other New England spider

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Bright yellow background with black depressions on top and variable red and black patterns underneath, creating a bold color scheme that's visible from several feet away

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds classic circular orb webs with sticky spiral threads that feel tacky to the touch when accidentally walked into, typically positioned between shrubs or trees

idTips.label: Spines
idTips.description: Six prominent tubercles (spiky bumps) project from the abdomen's edges, black-tipped with red bases, feeling hard and pointed if gently touched with a twig

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females are roughly the size of your pinky nail (9mm body length), while the rarely-seen males are about half that size and lack the dramatic spines

habitat: Look for Arrow-shaped Orbweavers in wooded areas, forest edges, and shrubby locations throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. They prefer spots where they can anchor their webs between branches of understory shrubs, young trees, or along woodland paths where there's enough space to build their circular webs but still some protection from wind.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; juveniles may be present but are much smaller and harder to identify reliably.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when mature females are most visible in their webs, displaying full adult coloration and size. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, with females still maintaining webs and showing bright colors before the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off after the first hard freeze; species overwinters as eggs or very young spiderlings in protected locations.

funFact: Despite their fearsome-looking spikes, these spiders are completely harmless to humans and their tubercles are actually made of the same material as their exoskeleton—they're like tiny built-in armor plates that may help protect them from being eaten by birds who mistake them for thorny plant parts!
confusionNotes: The spiky tubercles and bright yellow arrow shape make this spider nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in New England. The closest relatives are the Spined Micrathena and White Micrathena, but the Arrow-shaped's distinct triangular profile is unique—remember 'arrow equals triangle' as your memory trick.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Micrathena honors the Greek goddess Athena, known for her wisdom and skill in weaving—a fitting tribute to these master web-builders. Don't let the 'micro' part fool you though; while it means 'small,' these spiders are actually quite noticeable once you spot them!
compareHints: Among its Micrathena relatives in New England, the Arrow-shaped is the only one with a truly triangular, arrow-like abdomen. The Spined Micrathena has a more oval body with different spine arrangements, while the White Micrathena is predominantly white with a completely different color scheme. The Arrow-shaped's bright yellow background and geometric triangle shape make it the most distinctive of the three.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Arrow-shaped Orbweaver which has two prominent rear spikes, the Spined Micrathena bristles with multiple spines around its entire abdomen.
Compared to its relatives in the Micrathena genus, the White Micrathena is distinguished by its glossy black coloration with contrasting white markings and golden-brown legs.
